name: Reddish Black
lede: Reddish Black is one of the named blacks in the nomenclature that naturalists used to describe moth wings, ducks and ores before color photography.

sections.title: A black in Syme's list
sections.body:
In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a nomenclature of 54 colors to help identify minerals [1]. The Scottish artist Patrick Syme expanded it to 108 terms in 1814 and 110 in 1821, adding a painted swatch and example species from the animal, vegetable and mineral worlds [1]. Reddish Black is number 21 among the blacks in Syme's 1821 edition [2]. Baty's account places it among the blacks of Syme's own 1814 edition [2]. Our library files it under Werner's nomenclature, and the two accounts differ on that point [3].

The other blacks run from [[greyish-black]] and [[bluish-black]] through [[greenish-black]] and a brownish pitch black to ink black and velvet black [2].

sections.title: What it was matched to
sections.body:
Syme's examples for Reddish Black were the spots on the large wings of the tiger moth, the breast of the pochard duck, the berry of *Fuchsia coccinea*, and a mineral called olivenite, which Baty glosses as a copper arsenate [2]. His recipe mixed velvet black with a touch of carmine red and a little chestnut brown [2].

The recipe is a useful lesson. A dark like this reads as black until you place it beside a pure black, and then the warm cast shows.

sections.title: Other words for the same dark
sections.body:
Older English had Latin-derived words for it [4]. Paterson's dictionary lists *atrorubent* as reddish-black, and *fusco-piceous* as reddish black too [4]. The same dictionary has *atrosanguineous*, for the dark red of blood [4]. In mineralogy, the Pigment Compendium describes brookite, a titanium oxide named after H. J. Brook (1771 to 1857), as a brown or reddish black mineral [5].

Naturalist colors were also borrowed by doctors. Birren's list of colors of illness has frostbite passing from pale skin into dark red, reddish or reddish-black [6]. Baty reports that James Hunter's 1841 table of colors for an inflamed iris adopted Werner's nomenclature, and the terms printed in the extract include reddish black [7]. That last point rests on a single, partly garbled passage, so treat it as likely rather than certain.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here, #433635, is a scan of an aged Werner swatch [3]. It is very dark, at a lightness of 24 out of 100, with a slight red cast [3]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 20, and the nearest app color is [[umber]], 10.5 units away; [[chocolate-brown]] is the nearest named neighbor in the library [3]. The library's Japanese set pairs it with *dobunezumi*, which means brown-rat grey [3].

Because the swatch comes from an old printed chart, the tint may have shifted with age. Treat it as a scan, not a standard.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,249 works, 9.5 per cent [8]. It is a shadow color, playing that role in 81 per cent of the paintings that carry it [8]. The largest are portraits and heads. First is [[painter:bartholomeus-van-der-helst|van der Helst's]] [[painting:commons-Q30222055|Self-portrait]] of 1667, at 92 per cent of the canvas [8]. Neufchatel's *Portrait of an Elderly Man* of about 1550, also at 92 per cent, comes next [8]. Last is [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh's]] [[painting:commons-Q26220158|Head of a Young Peasant in a Peaked Cap]] of 1885, at 87 per cent [8].

It grows more common in later centuries: 226 of 1,674 works in the 1900s, 13.5 per cent, with the 1940s at 6 of 28 [8]. Norwegian paintings carry it in 25 of 120 works and Danish ones in 320 of 1,676 [8]. [[painter:carl-bloch|Carl Bloch]] has it in 8 of 15 works and [[painter:wilhelm-marstrand|Marstrand]] in 14 of 36 [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [8].
